name: Immanuel Kant
summary: Kant grounded politics in Right, the coexistence of free persons under law, and argued for a representative republic with separated powers, no hereditary privilege and a federation of free states for perpetual peace. He denied any right of revolution or resistance, defended retributive punishment including the death penalty, and kept women and economically dependent people out of the vote. His views on race and sex conflict with his universal doctrine of human dignity.

notes: Sources are his own texts in English (Hastie, Smith, Semple, Beck, Bernard) and German. Themes searched: government and law (Rechtslehre, Theory and Practice, Perpetual Peace), world (Perpetual Peace, Rechtslehre sec. 53-62, Universal History), liberty and punishment, religion (Religion, Enlightenment, Rechtslehre on church), society and race and gender (1764 Observations, 1775 and 1785 race essays). Not opened: the Metaphysics of Morals Doctrine of Virtue and Anthropology lectures, so duties to animals, suicide in the Doctrine of Virtue, and later gender and race remarks are unanswered. Mixed evidence (equal-moral-worth) is 0 at low. The Rechtslehre was read in the 1887 Hastie translation, which uses older terms such as 'paederasty'.
